This article is a review and meta-analysis (not an original fMRI study). It does not report primary fMRI data from healthy adult participants, meeting the exclusion criterion for systematic reviews/meta-analyses.

fMRI study in healthy 'normal volunteers' examining social processing (identification and attribution of others' emotions), directly relevant to perception/understanding of others. Abstract does not state participant ages; include for full-text review to confirm age range and other eligibility details.

Abstract describes methodological network analysis of functional connectivity related to psychosis risk; no indication that participants performed a social-related task or that social processing was assessed. Therefore it does not meet the fMRI social-task inclusion criterion.

Functional MRI study examining neural responses to nonverbal social stimuli (biological vs scrambled motion) tied to social-network complexity, addressing social perception/communication. Conducted in humans with no clinical groups mentioned, fitting inclusion criteria for fMRI social processing in healthy adults.

The study uses resting-state fMRI to examine connectivity biomarkers; the abstract does not describe any social-related task performed during scanning. Although healthy controls are included, it does not meet the inclusion requirement of task-based social processing.

fMRI study of social cognition (individuating vs categorical social judgments) in humans, meets review objective. Abstract does not specify participant ages/health status; not enough detail to confirm inclusion fully, so include for full-text review to verify healthy adult sample (17–65).

Abstract reports neural signatures of affective self- and other-touch (social-related processing: perception/understanding of self and others) comparing adults with ADHD and neurotypical controls, implying fMRI data. Includes a healthy adult control group. Not a review. Therefore meets inclusion criteria.

fMRI experiment examining social cognition (person perception and person knowledge) with participants performing social-related tasks. Abstract does not state participant age or health status; therefore include for full-text review to confirm healthy adults 17–65.

fMRI study with 78 healthy adult participants performing a task (reading narratives) that probes social-cognitive processing of protected values (engages mPFC, TPJ, posterior medial cortex). Fits 'Perception and Understanding of Others' social-related constructs and includes healthy adults; not a review.

Abstract is a narrative overview but specifically mentions the author’s early fMRI studies of social emotions in humans. The abstract lacks methods, participant ages, and whether healthy adults were scanned. Insufficient detail to confirm eligibility; include for full-text review to verify primary fMRI data in healthy 17–65-year-olds.

Primary empirical fMRI study examining prosocial (altruistic) choice and neural encoding of social attributes, addressing social-related processing. Not a review/meta-analysis and likely conducted in healthy adult participants. Meets inclusion criteria for social-processing fMRI studies.

fMRI social task but sample comprises early adolescent girls (adolescents), i.e., participants under age 17. Does not meet inclusion age range (17–65). Not a review/meta-analysis. Exclude based on age.

fMRI study where human participants performed an emotional classification task involving facial and vocal emotions—fits social communication/perception of others. Not a review/meta-analysis. Although participant ages/health not explicitly stated, study likely used healthy adults; include for full-text review to confirm sample details.

fMRI study with healthy adult participants performing a social-communication task (evaluating feeling of being addressed); reports neural activations related to social processing. Not a review. Fits inclusion criteria.

This is a conceptual primer/review about brain-imaging principles, not an original fMRI study. The abstract contains no evidence of an fMRI experiment or participants performing a social-related task; thus it does not meet the inclusion criteria.
This paper is a meta-analysis/systematic review of >200 fMRI studies rather than an original fMRI study in healthy adults, meeting the exclusion criterion.

Original fMRI study investigating person perception and mentalizing (social cognition) using human/robot avatars and belief manipulations in healthy adults. Task probes perception/understanding of others; not a review. Abstract provides sufficient information to meet inclusion criteria.

Study used an fMRI social-approval task (social reward processing) and included a healthy control group (15 controls). It examines social-related processing in humans during fMRI and is not a review. Age range not specified but participants are adults; criteria met for inclusion.

fMRI study in healthy adult participants investigating self-referential (social) processing (conceptual and agentic self) during task-based scans; directly addresses perception/understanding of self. Not a review/meta-analysis. Abstract provides sufficient information to include for full-text review.

Study involves fMRI of patients with mild traumatic brain injury during piano-based cognitive rehabilitation; no indication of social-related task or healthy adult participant group (17–65). Does not meet review focus on social processing in healthy adults.

Task-based fMRI included social processing (social cognition) alongside other tasks in a large sample from the Human Connectome Project (healthy adults). Meets inclusion criteria for social-related fMRI in healthy participants.

Participants are children (one high-functioning autistic child, one Asperger’s child, three normal children). Inclusion requires at least one group of healthy adults aged 17–65; this study does not meet the age criterion.

Study uses fMRI to examine executive control network hub architecture in autism during executive-demand tasks; the abstract does not describe any social-related task or social processing (e.g., affiliation, communication, self/other perception). Does not meet the review objective of social-related fMRI in healthy adults.

fMRI study where participants considered sharing news articles; neural activity linked to self-related processing and taking others’ perspectives (social cognition). Participants appear to be healthy adults and no exclusion criteria apply. Study directly examines social-related processing, so include for full-text review.

This paper is a narrative review of neuroimaging findings in autism rather than an original fMRI study with participants performing social tasks. It is a review article (excluded per criterion: systematic reviews/meta-analyses) and does not report primary fMRI data in healthy adults.

Abstract reports neural responses in human posterior superior temporal sulcus to stimuli depicting social interactions between agents, addressing social perception. Likely an fMRI study of healthy adults relevant to social processing. Insufficient explicit methods in abstract is minimal but context and journal make inclusion appropriate for full-text review.

Abstract reports an fMRI study of honesty-related neural signals that predict trust during social interactions, meeting the social-related task requirement. Participant health/age not specified in abstract, so include for full-text review to confirm eligibility.

fMRI study examining gaze-direction effects on face processing—a social attention/communication task. Abstract reports neural responses in fusiform, amygdala, and intraparietal sulcus, consistent with social-related processing in humans. Participant details/ages not specified, so include for full-text review to confirm healthy adult (17–65) sample.

This is a review article (Trends in Cognitive Sciences) about infant fMRI and cortical face-area development, not an original fMRI study of healthy adults (age 17–65) performing social tasks. It meets the exclusion criterion for systematic reviews and does not provide eligible adult fMRI data.

fMRI study of social cue processing (fearful faces with gaze) and includes a matched healthy adult control group (26 adults). Task assesses social perception/communication; fits inclusion criteria for fMRI social-related processing in adults.

fMRI task involved repeating words/pseudowords to study speech production and aging; no social task, interaction, or explicit social-communication manipulation is described. Mention of vocal imitation as socially relevant does not make the experimental paradigm a social-processing task.

Abstract reports a functional MRI study probing social-related processing (perception of others walking together) and reports activation of social brain areas. It matches the review objective. However, participant age/health status are not specified in the abstract, so include for full-text review to confirm presence of healthy adults (17–65).

fMRI study investigating attentional orienting to gaze (a social cue) and arrow cues; addresses social perception/understanding of others. Abstract does not state participant ages or explicitly that participants are healthy, so include for full-text review to confirm sample characteristics and eligibility.

fMRI study with 30 healthy adult participants performing communicative (social) vs descriptive speech tasks in L1/L2. Examines neural correlates of social communication (theory of mind/action simulation) in healthy adults, so meets inclusion criteria and is not a review.

fMRI study of mental-state decoding (Reading the Mind in the Eyes), a social cognition task (perception/understanding of others), conducted in healthy adult participants (native Japanese and white American). Not a review/meta-analysis. Fits the review objective and inclusion criteria.

fMRI was conducted while participants used Compassion-meditation and Reappraisal to modulate responses to film clips of people in distress, a social-related task involving affiliation/understanding others. Sample consists of human adult practitioners (healthy group). Study is empirical fMRI, not a review. Abstract provides sufficient information for inclusion.

The article is a review of seven structural/functional MRI studies in ADHD samples rather than a primary fMRI study of healthy adults. It is a review paper and focuses on clinical (ADHD) participants, so it does not meet inclusion criteria for fMRI social-processing studies in healthy adults.

Study uses resting-state and structural imaging rather than task-based fMRI of social processing, and participants are boys (children/adolescents; mean ages ~11–12, range 5.5–19.7) rather than healthy adults aged 17–65. It therefore does not meet the task-based fMRI or adult healthy participant inclusion criteria.

fMRI study administering a social interaction task (virtual ball-tossing/Cyberball) with a healthy control group (n=20) within adult participants; directly investigates neural processing of social-related stimuli and is not a review. Meets inclusion criteria.

Functional MRI study examining attributions about social situations (perception/understanding of others) in human participants, directly addressing the review objective. Abstract does not report participant ages/health status, so include for full-text verification; not a review.

fMRI study manipulating social cognitive load (social working memory) with neural activation sensitive to social processing and individual differences in perspective-taking. Appears to involve healthy adult participants and directly addresses social cognition processing. Not a review or meta-analysis.

fMRI study using the Prisoner’s Dilemma (a social interaction task) examining neural responses to cooperation/non-cooperation in (presumably) healthy adult participants; not a review or meta-analysis.

fMRI was conducted while participants viewed/listened to non-verbal facial and vocal stimuli, probing audiovisual social communication and perception of others. This is original empirical work (not a review) and fits the review’s social-processing fMRI focus. Abstract does not explicitly state ages, so full-text should confirm demographics.
Participants are described as adolescent girls (minors), not adults aged 17–65 required by the inclusion criteria; therefore the study does not meet the age criterion for inclusion.

This is an editorial/introduction to a special issue, not an original empirical fMRI study. The abstract describes the issue and other articles but reports no fMRI methods, participants, or social-task data; therefore it does not meet the inclusion criterion of a functional MRI study in humans.

Study reports task-based fMRI (generalized psychophysiological interaction during an emotional task) and includes a healthy control group (n=25). The abstract does not clearly state that the task probes social-related processing, so information is insufficient to exclude; include for full-text review to confirm relevance.

fMRI conducted while participants made social judgments (cooperator vs defector) learned through interactive Prisoner’s Dilemma — a social cognition task (perception/understanding of others). Appears to use healthy adult participants and is not a review. Abstract provides sufficient information for inclusion.

Study examines early adolescents (male and female adolescents) using fMRI; no evidence of any participant group within the required adult age range (17–65). Therefore it does not meet the inclusion age criterion for the review.

Abstract focuses on schizophrenia and cognitive remediation; it mentions social cognition but does not specify that an fMRI social-task was performed or whether healthy control participants (age 17–65) were included. Insufficient information to determine eligibility from abstract alone — include for full-text review.

fMRI study using a Theory of Mind task (social cognition) with an adult healthy control group (25 age- and gender-matched controls). Meets inclusion: social-related fMRI task and at least one healthy adult group. Not a review/meta-analysis. Abstract provides sufficient information for inclusion.

Abstract describes an overview/narrative review of molecular neuroimaging and neuroeconomics, not an original fMRI study with human participants performing a social task. Exclusion criterion met: systematic review/meta-analysis (review article). Insufficient as primary data for inclusion.

Abstract reports fMRI hemodynamic responses to child stimuli in neural regions associated with social cognition in human mothers. This fits social-related processing and involves adult human participants; no indication of being a review or excluding healthy adults. Sufficient information in abstract to include for full-text review.

fMRI study of processing emotional facial expressions (social-related task) and includes a healthy adult control group (mean age 27, within 17–65). Not a review/meta-analysis. Abstract provides sufficient information to include for full-text review.

fMRI study manipulating goal relevance during encoding and recognition of neutral faces; reports activation in social-processing region (superior temporal sulcus). Appears to involve healthy adult participants and is an original empirical study, not a review. Meets criteria for fMRI social-processing in healthy adults.

This is a narrative review of mirror neuron dysfunction in autism, not an original fMRI study reporting data from healthy adult participants. The study focuses on ASD populations and summarizes evidence from multiple modalities; it does not meet inclusion criteria requiring fMRI during social tasks in healthy adults.

fMRI study investigating perception of emotions and interactions in dynamic crowds—this is social-related processing (perception/understanding of others). Not a review; likely involves healthy adult participants. Meets inclusion criteria; sufficient info in abstract to include for full-text review.

fMRI study of social interaction (social exclusion) in human participants addressing social processing. Participants described as male adolescents but ages not specified; unclear if they meet 17–65 adult criterion. Include for full-text review to confirm participant ages and health status.
fMRI study of social cognition (Theory of Mind) that includes a healthy control group. Task involves social intention processing. No exclusion criteria met; suitable for full-text review.

Task-based fMRI in healthy male and female participants examining visual perception of social interactions (facing vs nonfacing body dyads), fitting 'Perception and Understanding of Others'. Not a review. Age not specified in abstract—include for full-text verification.

Event-related fMRI study examining processing of angry voice prosody (social communication), manipulating attention in healthy adult participants; addresses social cognition/perception of others. Not a review or meta-analysis. Abstract provides sufficient information to meet inclusion criteria for fMRI social-related processing in healthy adults.

Abstract reports an fMRI study measuring neural representations of others’ mental states in male and female human participants during social cognition tasks (perception/understanding of others). It fits the review’s social-processing constructs, involves healthy adult participants (not described as a patient sample), and is not a review or meta-analysis.

Abstract mentions oxytocin modulation of amygdala reactivity but does not specify that an fMRI social-related task was used or participant demographics. Insufficient information to confirm inclusion criteria; include for full-text review to determine task type and sample (healthy adults).
Resting-state fMRI in young children (age 3–7); no social-related task performed and participant sample is not healthy adults (17–65). Does not meet inclusion criteria.

Functional MRI was performed in 14 healthy adults (mean age 29±6) while they perceived others' emotional facial expressions—clearly a social-related task (perception/understanding of others). Not a review/meta-analysis. Meets inclusion criteria.

The study used resting-state fMRI, not task-based fMRI performed during a social-related task. Although healthy controls were included and behavioural ToM tests were administered, the inclusion criterion requires fMRI during a social task, so it does not meet criteria.

Empirical fMRI study (N=26) in healthy adults performing a social learning task (evaluating others' generosity) with a non-social control; investigates social-related processing and reports neural prediction-error signals. Not a review/meta-analysis. Meets inclusion criteria.

fMRI study in healthy adult participants (sighted and congenitally blind) performing voice-based identity and emotion recognition tasks, which target perception and understanding of others—a social processing construct. Not a review or meta-analysis. Abstract gives sufficient detail to meet inclusion criteria.

fMRI study includes a social cognition task (theory-of-mind / social attribution of belief) and reports scanning of human subjects. Not a review/meta-analysis. Abstract does not state ages explicitly, so full text should be checked for participant ages/health, but inclusion based on abstract is appropriate.

Abstract reports fMRI investigation of self- and other-processing in schizophrenia (a social-related task) but does not state whether a healthy control group (age 17–65) was included. No exclusion criteria clearly met. Insufficient information to determine inclusion from abstract alone — include for full-text review to confirm presence of healthy participants.

Narrative/theoretical review discussing mirror-touch synesthesia and fMRI evidence; does not report an original fMRI experiment conducted while participants performed a social-related task in healthy adults, so it fails the inclusion criterion requiring a functional MRI study.

Participants are adolescents (study focuses on depressed and healthy adolescents), not healthy adults aged 17–65 as required by the review objective. Although an fMRI social task (Cyberball) was used and a healthy group is present, the population age range does not match, so exclude.
Participants are infants aged 4–7 months, not healthy adults aged 17–65 as required by the review; therefore the study does not meet the participant age criterion for inclusion.

fMRI measured brain activity while healthy adult participants watched emotional/social movie scenes, engaging perception and understanding of others and social interaction. Task involves social-related processing; participants appear healthy; study is original research (not a review). Abstract provides sufficient info to include for full-text review.

This article is a review/reappraisal of social cognition in multiple sclerosis, summarizing neuropsychological and neuroimaging studies. It is not a primary task-based fMRI study of healthy adults. It therefore meets the exclusion criterion for systematic reviews/meta-analyses and does not provide evidence of an fMRI social task in healthy participants.

Study used structural MRI covariance analysis rather than task-based functional MRI; abstract does not describe an fMRI scan during a social task. Therefore it does not meet the inclusion criterion requiring a functional MRI social-task study.

fMRI experiment (N=31) measured neural responses while participants viewed photographs of disfigured faces — a social-perception task probing perception/understanding of others and social cognition (empathy). No indication study is a review or uses a clinical-only sample; likely healthy adults. Meets inclusion criteria for fMRI social processing in healthy adults.

fMRI study of healthy adult subjects observing toolmaking that explicitly investigates social-cognition processes (motor resonance, mentalizing, recognition of intentions). Not a review. Abstract lacks explicit ages but clearly meets the review objective; full text can confirm participant ages/health.

Study reports BOLD fMRI (3T) in 29 healthy adult participants (14F/15M) during processing of humorous cartoons — a social-cognitive task involving emotion appraisal and understanding others. Participants are within the adult age range and it is an original empirical fMRI study, not a review. Thus it meets inclusion criteria.

The study uses fMRI to investigate memory control and functional connectivity during a recognition task (mnemonic processes). It does not examine social-related processing (affiliation, communication, self/other perception), so it does not meet the review objective.

fMRI study with healthy late adolescents and young adults performing social scenarios; examines social-cognition and self-relevance regions. Includes an age group within 17–65 and meets task-related social processing criterion. Not a review.

fMRI was recorded while participants recalled World War II displays, a task probing collective/social memory and medial prefrontal social-cognitive processing. Abstract implies human participants likely healthy adults. Participant age/health not explicitly stated, so full text should be checked for eligibility; include for full-text review.

Functional MRI experiment investigating control of shared representations, self–other distinction, and mental state attribution — clearly a social-cognition task. Abstract implies human fMRI participants; participant health/ages not specified, so include for full-text review to confirm sample meets healthy adult criteria.

Participants are typically-developing children (mean age 10.1 years), whereas the review requires healthy participants aged 17–65. Although an fMRI social task was used, the sample does not meet the adult age inclusion criterion.

fMRI study where participants viewed and recognized actions (perception/understanding of others), a social cognition task. Abstract reports neural adaptation in pSTS, MT/MST, and EBA. Although ages not specified, the task and methods fit inclusion; include for full-text review to confirm participant demographics and ages.

fMRI study of neural mechanisms for simulating others’ decisions, clearly addressing social cognition (perception/understanding of others). Abstract does not specify participant health status or ages, so inclusion cannot be confirmed from abstract alone; include for full-text review to verify that at least one healthy adult group (age 17–65) was scanned.

Resting-state fMRI study in a sample of Major Depressive Disorder patients; no social task was administered and no healthy adult control group is reported. Does not meet inclusion criteria requiring task-based fMRI with (at least one) healthy participants aged 17–65.

Human fMRI study investigating representation/understanding of actions (auditory mirror system), i.e., perception/understanding of others—fits social-related processing. Appears to use healthy adult participants and is not a review. Age not specified in abstract, but insufficient grounds for exclusion; include for full-text review.

Study uses fMRI to examine prosodic speech (social communication), which fits social-related processing. However the abstract does not state whether a healthy adult control group (age 17–65) was included or provide participant ages. Insufficient information to confirm inclusion criterion—include for full-text review.

The study collected event-related fMRI while participants performed a mind-perception task and examined social-attention (gaze-cueing), which fits social-related processing. The abstract implies typical healthy adult participants; ages/health are not explicitly stated, so include for full-text review to confirm participant demographics and eligibility.

fMRI was performed with a healthy, non-clinical sample of young adult males who viewed and evaluated realistic social interaction scenarios (empathic processing). This is a social-related task (perception/understanding of others) in adults 17–65 and is not a review/meta-analysis. Abstract provides sufficient information to meet inclusion criteria.

fMRI study with healthy adult participants (n=26) performing a social-related task (observing human and robot experiencing pain/pleasure) probing empathy and social cognition. Not a review/meta-analysis. Abstract provides sufficient detail to meet inclusion criteria.

Empirical fMRI study of observation and mental imagery of meaningful face and limb movements, addressing social communication/perception of others. Not a review; appears to involve healthy adult participants. Task and imaging match inclusion criteria for social-related processing in healthy adults.

Abstract reports an fMRI study measuring neural responses to perception of facial expressions — a social communication task (perception/understanding of others). It appears to involve human participants and uses block-design fMRI. The abstract does not state participant ages or explicit health status; include for full-text review to confirm healthy adults (17–65).

Abstract reports an fMRI study investigating communicative intentions (social cognition) and neural systems underlying self/other-directed communication — directly relevant to social processing. The abstract does not specify participant ages or explicit healthy status; include for full-text review to confirm eligibility (healthy adults age 17–65).

Abstract reports neural activity during social communication in healthy pairs but does not specify the imaging modality (fMRI) or participant ages. Because the abstract lacks critical information about use of functional MRI, include for full-text review to determine eligibility.

Human fMRI study examining how learning about another person's values alters value representations and preferences (social influence). Involves social-related processing (perception/understanding of others) in humans; not a review. Likely healthy adult participants. Abstract provides sufficient info to include for full-text review.

Study used fMRI while adult mothers listened to their own/unfamiliar infant cry—a social/attachment-related task. Participants are adult primiparous mothers with no indication of psychiatric/neurological disorders. Fits inclusion criteria (social processing in healthy adults, ages likely 17–65). Not a review or meta-analysis.

Study examines neural responses to emotionally salient human eyes (mentalizing/social cognition) in adults and compares Tourette patients to healthy controls, indicating a social-related task with healthy adult participants; qualifies for full inclusion.

fMRI study examining neural mechanisms of interpersonal trust/distrust (social cognition). Sample of healthy adult participants (n=60). Task is social-related (control of attitudes toward others). Not a review or meta-analysis. Abstract provides sufficient information to meet inclusion criteria.

fMRI study of social cognition (charitable giving probing empathy, perspective taking, and attention shifts). Appears to involve healthy adult participants and is not a review. Age range not specified in abstract, so include for full-text review to confirm eligibility.

fMRI study where participants read passages varying in social content; investigates neural substrates of social cognition (dmPFC subnetwork) and links reading to social-cognitive performance. Appears to involve healthy adult participants and addresses perception/understanding of others. Not a review.

Abstract reports task-based fMRI including a social cognition task domain. Participant health status and ages are not specified in the abstract, so eligibility cannot be confirmed. Include for full-text review to verify presence of healthy adult participants (ages 17–65) and other eligibility details.

Functional MRI study with healthy adult participants (n=64) examining mentalizing/understanding of others (self–other anchoring-and-adjustment). Task is social cognition (inferring others' preferences). Not a review or meta-analysis. Satisfies inclusion criteria for fMRI social processing in healthy adults.

Participants were recruited from individuals entering psychotherapy for depression and/or anxiety; the abstract gives no indication of a healthy control group aged 17–65. Therefore it does not meet the requirement of including at least one healthy participant group.

fMRI study using a social interaction task (human-human competition) engaging Theory of Mind and executive processes in healthy subjects. Fits review objective of social processing in healthy adults. Not a review/meta-analysis. Age range not specified in abstract, but sufficient to include for full-text confirmation.

This is a resting-state functional connectivity study (no task performed during fMRI). Inclusion requires fMRI during a social-related task in healthy adults; the abstract reports no task-based social processing, so it does not meet inclusion.

fMRI study using the Human Connectome Project social cognition paradigm (a social-related task) that includes a matched healthy control group (n=25) performing the task. Meets inclusion criteria for social-related fMRI in healthy adults; not a review/meta-analysis.

The article is explicitly a systematic review of neuroimaging studies (not an original fMRI study of participants). It meets the exclusion criterion for systematic reviews/meta-analyses, so it should be excluded.

Study examines resting-state connectivity in cocaine-dependent individuals and relates to delayed discounting and reversal learning (cognitive/decision tasks), not social processing. It is not a task-based fMRI study of social-related processing, and participants are clinical (cocaine-dependent) rather than healthy adults. Abstract lacks any social cognition/social interaction task. Therefore it does not meet inclusion criteria.

fMRI hyperscanning study of dyadic social attention (mutual gaze and joint attention) in human participant pairs—directly addresses social processing. Abstract lacks explicit participant age range but likely healthy adults; insufficient detail on age warrants full-text review rather than exclusion.

This article is a meta-analysis of fMRI studies rather than an original fMRI study in human participants. The exclusion criteria specify systematic reviews or meta-analyses should be excluded, so this study is excluded.

fMRI study that explicitly includes a social-distance task (photographs of friends vs acquaintances) probing social familiarity/proximity to self. This addresses social processing in humans and likely involves healthy adult participants, meeting inclusion criteria for full review.

fMRI study investigating gesture-speech integration (social communication), includes healthy adult groups (replication group n=19 and matched controls n=17) performing a social-related task. Not a review/meta-analysis. Abstract provides sufficient detail to meet inclusion criteria.

Abstract reports fMRI mega-analysis of studies where participants considered others' mental states (social cognition). Not a review/meta-analysis. Participant health/ages not specified in abstract — include for full-text review to confirm eligibility.

Abstract describes case reports and a narrative review of ecstatic, orgasmic, and musicogenic seizures and related phenomena; mentions neuroimaging in epilepsy cases. No evidence of an fMRI study of healthy adults performing a social-related task. Appears not to meet inclusion criteria.

fMRI study measuring neural responses while participants viewed social-group photographs (social perception/understanding of others). Results report brain activations relevant to social cognition. Although ages/health status are not explicitly stated, the abstract clearly meets the social-related fMRI criterion; include for full-text review to confirm participant demographics and health.

Study investigates repetition effects and emotional memory (nonconscious recognition) using fMRI, not social processing. Task is a recognition memory paradigm with emotional photos, not a social-related task (affiliation, communication, self/other perception). Abstract provides no indication of social content or social cognitive processes. Therefore excluded.

fMRI study with an active task of listening to human footsteps engaging posterior STS (a 'social cognition' area), indicating social perceptual processing. Abstract lacks explicit participant health/age details, so full text is needed to confirm inclusion criteria. Include for full-text review.

fMRI study with healthy adult participants performing an affective creativity task (generating alternative appraisals for anger-evoking events), which taps emotion regulation and processes linked to social cognition (default-mode/social cognition hubs). Not a review. Abstract lacks explicit detail on interpersonal stimuli, so include for full-text review to confirm social-related processing.

fMRI study examining implicit false-belief processing (theory of mind), a social-cognitive task involving perception/understanding of others. Not a review/meta-analysis. Abstract does not explicitly state participant ages or health status, so full-text review recommended to confirm inclusion criteria (healthy adults 17–65).

The study used resting-state fMRI rather than a task-based social processing paradigm. Inclusion requires an fMRI scan while participants performed a social-related task; this criterion is not met despite measuring social functioning behaviorally. Therefore it should be excluded.

fMRI study using a Theory of Mind (social cognition) task and includes a matched healthy control group (n=13), satisfying the requirement of at least one healthy participant group. Ages not specified in the abstract; full text can confirm they fall within 17–65.
fMRI study of direct and reflected self-appraisals (social-related: perception/understanding of self) that includes a healthy adult group aged 23–30, meeting the inclusion criteria.

fMRI study where subjects encoded facts about unfamiliar people, showing person-selective ATL responses and connectivity with social cognition network—addresses perception/understanding of others. Abstract lacks explicit participant ages/health; include for full-text review to confirm eligibility.

Abstract summarizes fMRI work involving typically developing adults and social perception (STS), but it is a review of the authors’ research program and does not clearly state original fMRI methods/results for healthy adults in this paper. Insufficient detail to determine eligibility from abstract alone; include for full-text review.

Abstract reports training-induced changes in neural activation and connectivity in brain regions (DLPFC, nucleus accumbens) associated with social cognition/emotion, in healthy adults. Although fMRI is not explicitly named, the description of altered activation and connectivity strongly implies functional neuroimaging during social-related processing (responses to others' suffering), meeting inclusion criteria for fMRI studies of social processing.

fMRI study with healthy adult participants performing social-related tasks (attending to facial aspects, including emotional valence). Measures neural representation of social information; not a review/meta-analysis. Fits inclusion criteria.

fMRI study investigating social processing (pupil mimicry and trust) and activation of theory-of-mind network in human participants. Abstract does not specify participant ages or explicit healthy status, so include for full-text review to confirm eligibility (ages 17–65, healthy adults).

Abstract indicates this is a review article summarizing psychopharmacological and fMRI research rather than reporting original fMRI experiments in participants. It meets the exclusion criterion for systematic reviews/meta-analyses.

fMRI study using the Trust Game (a social dilemma) examining neural correlates of social decision-making in individuals with Machiavellian traits. No clinical populations are reported; likely healthy adult participants. Include for full-text review to confirm age and sample details.

fMRI conducted in healthy adult women (ages 25–50) during viewing of erotic pictures/videos. While primarily about sexual orientation and arousal, the task involves perception of others’ sexual stimuli — a form of social perceptual processing. Abstract is somewhat ambiguous regarding alignment with social-related constructs, so include for full-text review to confirm relevance.

Abstract reports neural tracking in frontal cortex during social interactions (cooperation/competition) and self–other representations, consistent with an fMRI social-processing task in healthy adults. The abstract does not explicitly state imaging modality or participant ages, so include for full-text review to confirm eligibility.

Abstract describes a review/perspective on social neuroscience rather than reporting an original fMRI study with human participants performing a social-related task. Does not meet the inclusion criteria for primary fMRI studies.

This is a narrative review/chapter summarizing amygdala findings across neurodevelopmental disorders and appraising existing structural and functional imaging literature, not an original fMRI experiment in healthy adults performing social tasks.

fMRI study investigating social communication (vitality forms) in humans, directly relevant to the review objective. Abstract describes task-based fMRI of action and speech processing. Participant health status and ages not specified, so include for full-text review to confirm eligibility (healthy adults 17–65).

fMRI was conducted while participants performed a scanner-adapted Multifaceted Empathy Test (a social cognition/empathy task). The study includes a healthy control group (age-/gender-matched controls) alongside a BPD group, meeting participant criteria. Not a review.

Abstract reports fMRI evidence of neural responses to MHC peptide-modified body odour and behavioral tests on recognition/‘self’ vs ‘non-self’ evaluation—this is social-related processing in healthy volunteers. Age range not specified; include for full-text review to confirm demographics/methods.

This is a resting-state fMRI study (no social-related task performed during scanning). Although it includes healthy adult participants, inclusion requires a task-based fMRI social paradigm; the abstract does not report one.

Participants were all individuals with alcohol use disorder (no healthy control group). The inclusion criteria require at least one group of healthy participants aged 17–65; this study contains only AUD participants (ages 24–66), so it does not meet the criterion.

Original fMRI study using a social interaction task (reaction-time competition with opponents and provocation/punishment), investigating reactive aggression — a social process involving responses to others. Human participants (adults) underwent fMRI; not a review. Meets inclusion for social-related fMRI in healthy adults based on abstract.

fMRI study with 34 healthy participants performing an empathic accuracy task (social cognitive processing — perception/understanding of others) during scanning. Not a review/meta-analysis. Age range not specified in abstract, so include for full-text confirmation of ages and other details.

fMRI study with human participants (n=14) performing a social-perception task (observing others' pupil dynamics), engaging regions involved in social salience. fMRI conducted during a face-recognition task (social perception/understanding of others), meeting the review’s social-processing and task-based fMRI criteria. fMRI study investigating agency inferences (perception/understanding of self), which falls under social-related processing. Includes a healthy control group (31 participants). Abstract lacks specific ages but likely adults; include for full-text review to confirm age range and extract data.

fMRI study of social (Theory of Mind/mentalizing) processing including a typically developing (healthy) group. Task-based fMRI examining perception of others (faces varying in race and socioeconomic status), addressing social cognition. fMRI study with 44 healthy participants performing explicit social trait judgments (trustworthiness, attractiveness) on voices—directly addresses social-related processing in healthy adults. fMRI study with 30 healthy adult participants performing a social-related task (direct vs. averted gaze) assessing neural measures of social processing (TPJ connectivity) and action control. Meets inclusion criteria (social task, healthy adults). Not a review or meta-analysis.

fMRI study with healthy participants performing a familiarity judgment of personally familiar vs famous/unfamiliar faces—addresses social perception/understanding of others. Age range not specified in abstract, so include for full-text review to confirm age eligibility and extract details.

fMRI study with 42 healthy adult participants performing a social-related task (self vs. other processing using romantic partner video vignettes). Fits inclusion criteria (social processing, healthy adults 17–65); not a review or meta-analysis.

fMRI study of anticipatory interpersonal touch comparing human vs fake hand — a social sensorimotor task relevant to social processing. Not a review. Abstract lacks explicit participant age/health details, so include for full-text review to confirm eligibility.

fMRI study of social processing (direct vs averted gaze; theory-of-mind/gaze perception). fMRI study with healthy sighted adult participants performing action perception/recognition and motor pantomime tasks engaging the mirror system — fits 'Perception and Understanding of Others' social processing. Not a review. Meets inclusion criteria.

fMRI study using a social contingency task probing self-relevant social reward processing; includes a healthy, age-matched neurotypical adult control group (24 TD adults, within adult age range). Fits social processing constructs and meets inclusion criteria.

fMRI study of social-related processing (empathizing with emotional faces) including a healthy typically developing control (TDC) group. fMRI study of decision-making influenced by expert advice (social influence), examines social-cognition regions (TPJ) and valuation; includes healthy adult group (18+), within 17–65 range; not a review. Abstract provides sufficient info to meet inclusion criteria.

Event-related fMRI in 51 healthy adults performing emotional sentence classification involving social cognition/Theory-of-Mind (affective speech comprehension). Fits inclusion criteria (social-related task in healthy adults) and is not a review. Abstract gives sufficient detail for inclusion.

fMRI study in 46 healthy adult volunteers performing theory-of-mind tasks (emotion, belief, pain) — directly examines social cognition/perception of others. Not a review/meta-analysis. Abstract provides sufficient info to meet inclusion criteria.

Primary fMRI study with 27 healthy adult participants performing a social-related task (observing cooperative vs affective interactions) probing intention understanding/mentalizing and action understanding. Fits the review objective and inclusion criteria; not a review or meta-analysis.

fMRI study examining social-cognitive processing (animacy/mentalizing) using animated figures; reports neural responses in social brain networks. fMRI study with healthy adults performing social-related tasks (SELF vs OTHER emotion attribution) probing empathy and perception/understanding of others. fMRI study with human listeners performing auditory emotion discrimination (social communication/perception of others), consistent with social-related processing in adults; not a review/meta-analysis. Abstract implies healthy participants. Included for full-text extraction.

fMRI study examining face/social-emotional processing (attention to eyes) with 20 neurotypical matched controls (healthy adults) and 20 ASD; task is social-related (perception/understanding of others); participants are young adults within 17–65. Not a review.

fMRI study of social processing (empathy/sympathy) in a healthy sample that includes adults (ages 7–40, so participants ≥17 present). fMRI study of social-related processing (direct and reflected self/other evaluations). Includes a healthy young adult group (ages 22–31), which falls within 17–65. Not a review—meets inclusion criteria.

fMRI study of social processing (joint attention, face processing, theory-of-mind/action networks) that includes neurotypical (healthy) control participants. Abstract does not specify participant ages (17–65 required), so full-text review needed to confirm age eligibility and other details.

fMRI study in adult human participants investigating socially-induced cognitive emotion regulation involving a psychotherapist (social cognition/attachment). fMRI study of social-related processing (implicit facial emotion task: fearful vs neutral faces — perception/understanding of others). Includes a healthy adult control group (24 matched controls). Not a review. Therefore meets inclusion criteria.

fMRI study with 22 healthy adult male participants performing social-related tasks (allocentric social hierarchy and social alliance judgments). fMRI study of cross-modal person recognition (voice-face priming) addressing perception/understanding of others, a social-related process. This is an animal study focusing on birdsong (songbirds) and discusses fMRI in songbirds; no human participants (age 17–65) performing social-related tasks are reported. Therefore it does not meet the review’s human fMRI inclusion criteria.

Human fMRI study with healthy adult participants (men, n=10 per group) performing social-related tasks (viewing romantic images—affiliation/attachment). Fits inclusion criteria (social processing in healthy adults). Not a review or meta-analysis.

Randomized, placebo-controlled fMRI study examining neural and behavioral responses during a social-interaction task (Prisoner’s Dilemma) in healthy adult males and females. Directly addresses social processing in healthy adults and is not a review; meets inclusion criteria.

Study used fMRI while participants viewed fearful faces (a social-emotional processing task). Includes a healthy adult control group matched to premutation carriers. Not a review/meta-analysis. Satisfies inclusion criteria for social-related fMRI in adults.

fMRI study in 37 healthy adult participants performing a social-evaluative task (watching approving/disapproving social videos), which targets social processing (perception/understanding of others). Not a review/meta-analysis. Abstract provides sufficient info to meet inclusion criteria.

Participants are children (middle childhood, ages 8–12); the meta-analysis requires at least one healthy adult group aged 17–65. Abstract gives no indication of adult participants, so it does not meet the age criterion.

fMRI study examining theory-of-mind/social exchange processing (social-related task). Abstract indicates neuroimaging of social cognition and activation of ToM areas. Participant health/ages not explicitly stated; include for full-text review to confirm healthy adult sample (17–65).

Abstract reports fMRI investigation of facial emotion processing in individuals at clinical high risk for psychosis—this is a social-related task. The abstract does not clearly state whether a healthy control group (age 17–65) was included. Insufficient information to confirm healthy participants, so include for full-text review to determine eligibility.

The study used resting-state fMRI rather than a task-based social processing paradigm, and no measures of social behavior/processing were reported. Although healthy controls were included, it does not meet the requirement of a social-related task.

The article is explicitly a review and meta-analysis of behavioral and neuroimaging studies; it is not an original fMRI study of healthy adults performing social tasks. It therefore meets the exclusion criterion for systematic reviews/meta-analyses.

This is a review article summarizing ERP and fMRI findings rather than an original fMRI study reporting primary data. It therefore meets the exclusion criterion for reviews/meta-analyses and does not provide evidence of conducting an fMRI social-task with healthy adult participants.

Abstract does not report that participants performed a social-related task; study focuses on resting-state parcellation and task-related coactivation/meta-characterization. Although 'social cognition' is mentioned in functional labeling, it is unclear whether original fMRI involved a social task. Insufficient detail to exclude—include for full-text review to determine whether social-task fMRI in healthy adults was performed.

fMRI was resting-state functional connectivity only, not a task-based fMRI during a social-related task. Although healthy controls and behavioral social cognition measures were included, the study does not meet the requirement of an fMRI scan conducted while participants performed a social-related task.

Event-related fMRI in healthy nulliparous adult women (n=17) using infant cries and faces—social stimuli tapping affiliation/attachment, perception of others, and reward processing. Fits inclusion criteria (social-related task; healthy adults 17–65). Not a review/meta-analysis.

Abstract describes imaging of ToM and empathy in schizophrenia patients but does not state whether fMRI during social tasks was used or whether a healthy control group (age 17–65) was included. Insufficient information to exclude—include for full-text review.

Abstract describes fMRI connectivity in autism spectrum disorder and clinical severity; it does not report fMRI during a social-related task in healthy adults nor mention a healthy 17–65 group. Focus is clinical ASD, not the review’s social-processing in healthy adults.

The study used resting-state fMRI with the social manipulation (critical remarks) presented before scanning rather than a social task performed during the fMRI. Inclusion requires fMRI during a social-related task; this does not clearly meet that criterion despite healthy adult sample.

The study used task-based fMRI during social-related processing (emotion recognition and gaze integration). It includes a healthy younger participant group aged 17–27 (within the 17–65 inclusion range). It is an original empirical fMRI study, not a review.
Study examines children and adolescents with autism spectrum disorder; no healthy adult (17–65) participant group is reported. Population and age range do not match the review’s inclusion criteria.

Abstract reports fMRI connectivity analysis of emotional processing in pre-manifest Huntington's disease, but does not specify that the fMRI was during a social-related task nor that healthy adult participants (age 18–65) were included. No exclusion criteria met. Include for full-text review to confirm presence of healthy control group and social-related task.

Abstract reports fMRI during a facial emotion perception task (social processing) and includes a healthy control group without MDD. Participant ages (18–65) are not specified in the abstract, so I2 is not fully demonstrated. Include for full-text review to confirm age eligibility.

Exclusion: none (not a review). Inclusion met: I1 (fMRI during anticipated peer evaluation—a social processing task). Inclusion not met: I2 (participants are pediatric/adolescents; no healthy adult [18–65] group demonstrated). Therefore excluded from review of healthy adults.

Abstract reports an fMRI study requiring participants to select between self and another's visual perspectives (a social-related task), satisfying I1. It does not specify participant ages or explicitly state participants were healthy adults 18–65, so I2 is not confirmed from the abstract. Not a review/meta-analysis (E1 not met). Include for full-text review to confirm I2.

Abstract does not specify that an fMRI scan was conducted during a social-related task or that participants were healthy adults aged 18–65. Title suggests neural imaging and social stimuli but provides insufficient detail to confirm inclusion criteria; no exclusion criteria identified. Include for full-text review to determine I1 and I2.

Abstract reports an fMRI study using the social Theory of Mind task (Reading the Mind in the Eyes Test), satisfying I1. It mentions a non-clinical (healthy) cohort but does not report participant ages, so I2 (age 18–65) is not confirmed from the abstract. No exclusion criteria are met. Because age information is insufficient, include for full-text review to confirm I2.

Exclusion IDs met: none. Inclusion IDs met: none. Inclusion IDs not met/not demonstrated: I1 (required social-related task during fMRI — this study used resting-state fMRI, no task), I2 not demonstrated (abstract does not explicitly state participants were healthy adults aged 18–65).

Meets I1: fMRI during a social-related Theory of Mind task. Abstract reports 109 healthy volunteers but does not specify participant ages (18–65) so I2 cannot be confirmed from abstract alone. No exclusion criteria met. Include for full-text review to confirm age range and other eligibility details.

The task is a precision visuomotor gripping (sensorimotor) task, not a social-related task (I1 not met). Participants are individuals with ASD with no clear healthy adult (18–65) group reported (I2 not met). Not a systematic review (E1 not met).

Abstract reports task-related BOLD signal within the face-processing network and involves healthy adult participants (ages ~22–26), but it does not explicitly state that fMRI was acquired during a social-related task. No exclusion criteria met. Include for full-text review to confirm whether a social task was used.

Excluded because the study used resting-state fMRI (no task), so it does not assess social-related processing. Exclusion IDs met: none. Inclusion IDs met: none. Inclusion IDs not met or not demonstrated: I1 (no social task; resting-state fMRI), I2 (healthy participants present but ages 18–65 not reported).

No healthy adult participants (I2 not met): sample described as 'boys' (likely minors), so age 18–65 not demonstrated. The study does meet I1 (fMRI during a social-related encoding task). No exclusion criteria are met (E1 not applicable). Therefore excluded for not satisfying inclusion criterion I2.

Exclusion IDs met: none. Inclusion IDs met: none. Inclusion IDs not met: I1 — this study used resting-state fMRI and diffusion imaging, not a task-based social processing fMRI; I2 — participants were adolescents (ASD and TD), not healthy adults aged 18–65. E1 (review/meta-analysis) not applicable.

Study uses resting-state fMRI, not a social-related task (I1 not met). Participants are youth aged 8–15, not healthy adults 18–65 (I2 not met). Not a review/meta-analysis (E1 not met). Therefore excluded based on I1 and I2 not demonstrated.

No social task — study used resting-state fMRI in adolescents (I1 not met). Participants are adolescents with ASD from ABIDE; no healthy adult group aged 18–65 reported (I2 not met). No exclusion criteria (e.g., review/meta-analysis) applied.

No exclusion criteria met. Inclusion criteria met: none. Inclusion criteria not met or not demonstrated: I1 (task is phonological memory/sign-language processing, not a social-related task such as social communication or perception), I2 (participant health status and ages not specified in abstract).

fMRI study in healthy adult participants examining observation and imitation of communicative (social) gestures, meeting I1 (social-related fMRI task) and I2 (healthy participant group). No exclusion criteria met from abstract.

Abstract does not specify that an fMRI scan was conducted nor clearly state participant health status/ages, so inclusion criteria cannot be confirmed from the abstract alone. No exclusion criteria are met. Include for full-text review to determine I1 (fMRI during social-related task) and I2 (healthy adults 18–65).

fMRI studies probe ATL responses to famous people and abstract social terms, indicating social-related processing during scanning (meets I1). Participant health/ages not specified in abstract, so include for full-text review.

E1 met: Abstract describes a review/meta-analysis of 103 brain-imaging studies. Inclusion: I2 met—mentions healthy volunteers and healthy control adults. I1 not met/not demonstrated—this is not an original fMRI study conducting social-related tasks; although 'social cognition' is mentioned, no specific fMRI social-task data in the abstract. Exclude due to E1.

Excluded because the study reports resting-state fMRI in youth with autism, not a task-based social fMRI study in healthy adults. Exclusion IDs met: none. Inclusion IDs met: none. Inclusion IDs not met/demonstrated: I1 (no social task fMRI), I2 (participants not healthy adults 18–65).

The study used fMRI during a social cognition task (modified Sally-Anne false-belief task) and included a group of typically developing (healthy) adult male participants as controls. No exclusion criteria are met in the abstract.

Abstract indicates study of social interactive deficits in BPD but does not specify that an fMRI social task was used or that healthy adult participants (age 18–65) were included. Insufficient information to determine inclusion; include for full-text review.

No exclusion criteria met. Does not satisfy inclusion criteria: I1 not met — study uses resting-state fMRI, not a social-related task; I2 not met — sample is autism spectrum disorder participants, no healthy adult (18–65) group reported. Therefore excluded based on failure to meet required inclusion criteria (I1, I2).

fulltext_screening_results.reason: This is an fMRI study in healthy adult participants (N=30, mean age 26) that uses a social-related body perception task probing perception and understanding of self and others. The authors report whole-brain, voxelwise group-level task activation analyses (FEAT/FLAME) with thresholded Z-statistic maps and coordinate results for contrasts (e.g., own body > scrambled; same-sex and opposite-sex other bodies) clearly from the healthy/control sample. Analyses include within-group and between-sex comparisons and parametric whole-brain results. The study is empirical, not ROI-only, and fits the review’s constructs (Perception/Understanding of Self and Others). Therefore it meets all inclusion criteria.

This is an fMRI study of social-related processing (understanding others’ regret) involving healthy adult participants (two samples of N=24, ages within 18–65). The paper reports group-level, whole-brain voxelwise task activation analyses (SPM5; contrasts IP−IF and OP−OF; parametric and conjunction analyses; thresholding and reported activation foci/coordinates), not limited to ROI, connectivity-only, or clinical groups. Whole-brain results for the healthy/control group are clearly described in the text and figures/tables. Therefore all inclusion criteria are met and no exclusion criteria are violated.

Although the study includes a healthy adult control group (N=24, ages 19–36) and uses task fMRI of social processing, the reported results are primarily between-group contrasts and ROI analyses. The paper does not present a clear, unmasked whole-brain group-level task activation map or contrast explicitly identified as coming from the healthy/control group alone. Whole-brain figures and tables focus on group interactions and BPD>HC or HC>BPD contrasts; the amygdala result is an ROI finding. Because the review requires at least one healthy-group whole-brain task-evoked statistical map (reported as HC task effect or within-group contrast), this study does not meet that inclusion criterion.

Meets all inclusion criteria: (1) Uses task-based fMRI to investigate perception of social interactions (social communication / perception of others). (2) Sample = 21 healthy adults (ages 18–35) with results reported for the healthy group. (3) Whole-brain analyses were performed and reported (whole-brain beta maps, group-level t-tests, and whole-brain searchlight analyses are described), providing voxelwise task-evoked results for the healthy sample. The study is empirical and not limited to ROI-only or connectivity-only analyses. No exclusion criteria are violated. Therefore the study should be included for the meta-analysis of fMRI studies of social-related processing in healthy adults.

This is an fMRI study of social interaction perception in healthy adult participants (Experiment 1: N=50, ages 19–34; Experiment 2: N=23, ages 18–30). The task probes perception/understanding of others (observed social interactions), satisfying the social-related construct. The paper reports group-level whole-brain task-evoked contrasts (e.g., social interaction > independent actions) with FDR-corrected clusters and surface-based group analyses, clearly from the healthy/control sample. It is empirical fMRI work (not ROI-only, not resting-state), and reports whole-brain results; therefore it meets all inclusion criteria and violates no exclusion criteria.

This is an empirical fMRI study in healthy adults (n=25, mean age 25.1) investigating social-related processing (learning about others’ preference similarity to self—affiliation/social cognition). The paper reports group-level, whole-brain voxelwise task-evoked results (cluster-corrected activations, peak MNI coordinates, conjunction analyses) rather than only ROI or connectivity analyses. Healthy participants’ whole-brain task contrasts and parametric modulators are clearly described and reported. No exclusion criteria apply (not ROI-only, not resting-state, participants are within 18–65). Therefore it meets all inclusion criteria for the review.

While this is an fMRI study of social processing (Cyberball) in adult participants (mean age ~19.8) and reports whole-brain, group-level activation maps (EX–IN and SUP–EX), the reported whole-brain results are for the entire sample (46 participants), which includes 9 participants meeting criteria for social anxiety disorder. The paper does not present a clearly identified whole-brain group-level task activation map coming specifically from a healthy/control-only group. The review’s eligibility rules require that if clinical participants are included, results for the healthy group must be reported separately (or a whole-brain healthy/control map must be clearly identified). Because that criterion is not met, the study must be excluded.

Although the study uses task fMRI with healthy adult controls and addresses social-affective processing, it does not report any group-level whole-brain (voxelwise) task-evoked statistical map for the healthy/control group. Analyses are based on predefined network nodes and sliding-window network cohesion indices (ROI/network-level connectivity) and comparisons of these NCI time series; no unmasked whole-brain healthy-group activation maps or voxelwise contrasts are presented. This falls under the exclusion criterion for studies reporting only ROI/network or connectivity analyses without whole-brain task activation results. Therefore it fails the ‘whole-brain evidence’ inclusion criterion.

The study used task-based fMRI of a social-related paradigm (peer-oriented social judgment assessing acceptance/rejection), meeting the construct of social reward/processing. It includes a healthy adult control group (n=20; mean age ~28) and reports within-group, whole-brain, voxelwise task-evoked contrasts for the control group (acceptance>control and rejection>control). Analyses were whole-brain (SPM8) with cluster-based correction and results for the healthy/control group are described in the text and figures. The paper is empirical, not ROI-only, resting-state, or connectivity-only, and reports unmasked whole-brain healthy-group task activations. Therefore it meets all inclusion criteria and violates none of the exclusion criteria.

This paper reports task-based fMRI of action observation and weight-discrimination (perception/understanding of others’ actions), which falls under 'Perception and Understanding of Others' (a social-related construct). Multiple experiments include healthy adult participants (n=79 across Experiments 1–3; separate healthy control group n=31 reported for the clinical comparison), with results for healthy groups reported separately from the SCA6 patients. The manuscript presents group-level, voxelwise task activation contrasts (e.g., ActionOBS–CtrlOBS; Sleeve/NoSleeve contrasts) and statistical maps/analyses (thresholds, conjunctions, ROI and whole-brain comparisons) clearly attributed to the healthy/control groups. Thus it meets the review’s fMRI, sample, and whole-brain evidence inclusion criteria.

Although this is an fMRI task study of social processes in healthy adult physicians (n=18) and the task/behavioral measures map onto social constructs (empathic concern/compassion), the reported neuroimaging results are from an a priori ROI-restricted analysis (5mm spheres) with FWE correction performed within those ROIs. The paper does not present an unmasked, whole‑brain group-level task-evoked statistical map (voxelwise whole‑brain results) for the healthy group. Because the review’s inclusion criteria require at least one group-level whole‑brain (voxelwise) task activation map, this study must be excluded despite meeting other criteria.

Although this is an fMRI study of social-related processing (biological motion) that includes a healthy adult control group, it does not report a clear group-level, whole-brain (voxelwise) task activation map for the healthy/control group. The paper relies on individual-level ROI localizers (STSp and MT), ROI-based event-related analyses, and reports ROI peak activations and Talairach coordinates. Whole-brain analyses described were directed at patients (searching for clusters) and no unmasked, group-level healthy-control whole-brain contrast or coordinate table of healthy-group task activations is provided. Thus it fails the requirement for healthy-group whole-brain task-evoked results and must be excluded.

Although the study uses a social task (interactive Domino) and includes a healthy adult control group (n=30, ages 18–34), the paper does not clearly report an unmasked, whole‑brain, group-level task-evoked statistical map (voxelwise GLM contrast) explicitly identified for the healthy/control group. The analyses center on ICA-derived component spatial maps and between-group comparisons of component beta-weights (temporal-sorting), with component maps reportedly created from back-reconstructed ICs across all participants rather than a TD-only whole-brain task activation map or coordinate table for the healthy group. Because the inclusion criteria require at least one clearly identified whole-brain (voxelwise) task effect for the healthy/control group, this study does not meet criterion #3 and must be excluded.

This is an empirical fMRI study in healthy adult participants (n=20; mean age ~20.6) that investigates event simulation and explicitly addresses social-cognition constructs (theory of mind, trait inference) and uses stimuli that include social situations (~42% social). The paper reports whole-brain, group-level voxelwise analyses (second-level random-effects one-sample t-tests) with cluster-corrected thresholds (p<0.001 height, p<0.05 cluster) and coordinates for activation peaks (and additional reported uncorrected peaks). Tasks involved explicit/implicit situational understanding and future prediction, producing contrasts (e.g., Exp–Imp, Ftr–Exp) that identify canonical social brain regions (MPFC, TPJ, TP, PCC). All inclusion criteria are met and no exclusion criteria apply.

This is a task-based fMRI study of action observation/execution in healthy adults (final N=12, mean age 26), directly addressing perception/understanding of others’ actions (inferring others’ applied force). The paper reports group-level, whole-brain voxelwise task analyses (SPM12 GLM, polynomial parametric modulation), whole-brain statistical maps, tables of coordinates, and conjunction/second-level results for the healthy sample. It is not ROI-only, not limited to connectivity/resting-state, and reports unmasked healthy-group task effects. Therefore it meets all inclusion criteria (social-related fMRI task; healthy adult sample; whole-brain group-level task results) and violates no exclusion criteria.

The study is an fMRI hyperscanning experiment of real-time mutual eye contact—a clearly social communication task. Participants are healthy adults (n≈30, mean age ~21.7), within the 18–65 range. The paper reports group-level, whole-brain task-evoked analyses (GLM contrasts LIVE > REPLAY) with cluster-level FWE correction and provides regional results (tables/figures), satisfying the whole-brain evidence requirement. Although additional connectivity and interbrain synchronization analyses are included, the study also presents univariate whole-brain activation maps for the healthy sample, and results are not restricted to ROIs or to only connectivity/resting analyses. Therefore all inclusion criteria are met and no exclusion criteria apply.

Although this fMRI study includes a healthy adult control group and probes a social-related process (irony comprehension—social communication/perception of others), the full text does not present an unmasked, whole-brain, group-level task activation map clearly identified as coming from the healthy/control group. The reported neuroimaging results focus on between-group contrasts (controls > schizophrenia and reverse) and combined/previously published control results; main effects are described for “study participants” without providing a standalone whole-brain healthy-group map (coordinate table or figure) in this paper. Because the review requires at least one clearly reported healthy-group whole-brain task-evoked statistical map, this manuscript does not meet the whole-brain evidence inclusion criterion and must be excluded.

This is a task-based dual‑fMRI (hyperscanning) study of social interaction (cooperation vs competition), conducted in healthy adults (n=38; mean age 22.4). The analyses produce group-level whole-brain spatial components from gICA (voxelwise maps shown/used) and report task-related effects via back-reconstructed component time‑courses and group statistical tests (paired t-tests, ISC comparisons). The paper is not ROI-only, not resting-state-only, and reports healthy-group whole‑brain results tied to task conditions. Therefore it meets the review’s inclusion criteria.

The study uses fMRI during social-related tasks (self-reflection and other-reflection — constructs of Perception/Understanding of Self and Others). It includes a healthy adult control group (21 HCs) reported separately. The paper reports group-level whole-brain task effects for the healthy control group (main effects in HCs: VMPFC, DMPFC, ACC, PCC, precuneus, etc.), with thresholds and results summarized (including Supplementary Table S1), i.e., whole-brain voxelwise activations rather than ROI-only analyses. No exclusion criteria are met (not resting-state/seed-only, not ROI-only, includes healthy adult group). Therefore it meets all inclusion criteria for the meta-analysis.

Meets all inclusion criteria: task is an fMRI task involving observation of others’ actions with risk—relevant to social perception/understanding; sample comprises healthy adult participants aged 18–22 (within 18–65); group-level whole-brain voxelwise task contrasts (risk-taking vs safe) were computed and reported using SPM (maps, coordinates and figures are provided); the paper is empirical and not ROI-only, connectivity-only, or resting-state only, and results for the healthy group are reported. No exclusion criteria are violated. The study therefore qualifies for inclusion in the meta-analysis of fMRI studies of social-related processing in healthy adults.

This is an fMRI study of social-related processing (empathy toward humans and animals) in healthy adult participants (n=60, ages 18–60). The paper reports group-level, whole-brain voxelwise task contrasts (human negative > neutral; animal negative > neutral) with second-level random-effects analyses and coordinates with FWE-corrected thresholds and conjunction/within-group maps. Healthy groups’ whole-brain results are clearly reported separately (within-group and between-group contrasts). The study is empirical, not ROI-only, not resting-state or connectivity-only, and participants fall within the 18–65 range. Therefore it meets all inclusion criteria and violates no exclusion criteria.

This is an fMRI study of narrative comprehension that explicitly probes social-related processing (mentalizing/Theory-of-Mind). Sample: healthy adult participants (N=18, ages 18–27). The paper reports group-level whole-brain task contrasts (Mentalizing vs Action; Action vs Mentalizing) with appropriate multiple-comparison correction and reported cluster coordinates/locations, not limited to ROI-only results. The task evokes social cognition (perception/understanding of others) during story listening. No exclusion criteria are violated (not ROI-only, not resting-state/connectivity-only, healthy adult group reported separately). Therefore it meets all inclusion criteria for the meta-analysis.

This is an fMRI task study of social/affiliative processing (maternal attachment and owner-dog bond) using a passive viewing paradigm clearly targeting affiliation/attachment. Sample consists of healthy adult women (ages 22–45). The paper reports group-level, voxelwise SPM8 analyses and multiple within-group contrasts (e.g., own child vs. fixation, own dog vs. fixation, own child vs. own dog, own vs. unfamiliar) with activation maps and MNI coordinates provided. Although significance was assessed with ROI-based small-volume correction, the analyses were conducted voxelwise across normalized whole-brain data and results for the healthy adult group are reported and illustrated, meeting the review’s requirement for group-level whole-brain task-evoked maps/coordinates. No exclusion criteria (e.g., only ROI results, only connectivity/resting-state, non-adult sample) apply. Therefore the study should be included.

This is an fMRI study in healthy adults (N=18, ages 18–24) that reports group-level, whole-brain voxelwise task contrasts (Popular>Notes, Artistic>Notes, Popular>Artistic, Artistic>Popular) with voxelwise and cluster-level correction and coordinate tables. Although the task is aesthetic music appreciation rather than an explicit ToM task, the authors frame and demonstrate involvement of social-related processing (default mode/ToM and cognitive-empathy regions such as arMFC, PCC/PC, TPJ, hippocampus) and present whole-brain results for those contrasts in the healthy sample. Therefore it meets the sample, whole-brain reporting, and social-related processing relevance criteria (perception/understanding of others; cognitive empathy) for inclusion.

This is an fMRI task study of empathy for pain, a social/other-focused process (perception/understanding of others). The sample includes healthy adult participants in the 20–30 age range (meets 18–65 criterion) and reports results separately by age group. The paper reports group-level whole-brain task activation maps/contrasts (e.g., pain>no pain and pain>baseline) with voxelwise statistics (FWE-corrected maps and tables of coordinates) for the healthy participants; NeuroVault and coordinate tables are provided. Analyses are not limited to ROIs or connectivity only. Although an older group (65–75) is included, the younger healthy adult subgroup is analyzed and reported separately, satisfying the age-range requirement. Therefore the study meets all inclusion criteria and violates no exclusion criteria.

The study reports task-based fMRI of social processing (perception of others’ dynamic vs. static facial expressions). It includes a clearly reported healthy adult control group (n=13, age M=24.3) with results reported separately from the ASD group. Group-level whole-brain task contrasts for the control group (dynamic > static; and interaction contrasts) are presented with voxelwise statistics, corrected thresholds, and MNI coordinates (i.e., whole-brain random-effects maps), not limited to ROIs. Although the paper also reports connectivity/DCM and patient vs. control comparisons, it provides unmasked whole-brain activation maps for the healthy control group, satisfying all inclusion criteria and violating none of the exclusion criteria.

This is a task-based fMRI study of social cognition (approachability judgments), including a healthy adult control group. The paper reports within-group and between-group whole-brain task contrasts (social > gender and gender > baseline) and describes whole-brain voxelwise results for groups, with within-group analyses and statistical maps reported in the main text and supplementary materials (supplementary tables/figures). Results are not limited to ROI or connectivity analyses, and healthy-control group results are reported separately (within-group analyses and comparisons). Participants are adults and healthy controls are clearly defined. Therefore the study meets inclusion criteria for fMRI social-related processing with whole-brain healthy-group task activation maps.

This is an empirical fMRI study in healthy adult participants (N=23, ages 19–32) examining neural correlates of suspense during reading.
